Books price Denver home-court but underweight the physiological altitude penalty on visitor shooting.

name: altitude_visitor_unders_props
thesis: Visiting players in Denver (altitude 5280ft) see a measurable decline in second-half efficiency. Player points props for visitors should be priced lower than market implies. Specifically, visiting guards playing 30+ minutes see ~4% fewer points than their season average in Denver, creating systematic over on books that don't altitude-adjust. Test by comparing visitor player points outcomes vs. closing prop lines in DEN home games.

name: assist_inflation_vs_zone_defense
thesis: Player assists props are set off season averages but don't account for opponent defensive scheme. Teams that play 40%+ zone defense disrupt passing lanes and force isolation scoring, suppressing assists for primary ball handlers by 1.5-2.0 per game. Consensus devig should reveal 4%+ edges on assist unders for point guards facing zone-heavy defenses.

name: assists_boost_missing_teammate
thesis: When a team's secondary playmaker (top-3 in AST%) is ruled out, the primary ball handler's assists prop is adjusted upward by books but not enough — the consolidation of usage is sharper than priced. The OVER on primary handler assists hits at 57%+ when the #2 or #3 assist man is OUT, yielding 5%+ edge vs devigged consensus.

name: b2b_fatigue_player_props
thesis: Players on the second night of a back-to-back see a measurable drop in points, rebounds, and assists props relative to their season averages, but books anchor player lines to rolling averages that underweight the fatigue discount. Target unders on player_points and player_points_rebounds_assists for starters logging 30+ minutes on zero-rest games, especially road B2Bs where travel compounds the effect.

name: b2b_rest_asymmetry_rebounds
thesis: When a team on a back-to-back faces an opponent with 2+ days rest, the rested team's starting center averages +1.8 rebounds above their season line. Books price the spread adjustment for fatigue but do not proportionally adjust individual rebound props for the rested big. Target: overs on rested team center rebounds when opponent is on a back-to-back.

name: b2b_rest_rebound_mismatch
thesis: When a team on a back-to-back faces a fully rested opponent (3+ days rest), the rested team's primary center/PF outperforms their rebound prop by ~1.2 boards on average. Fatigued teams contest fewer rebounds and box out less aggressively, especially in Q3/Q4. The edge is strongest when the B2B team also traveled (not home-home). Books price rebound props off season averages without sufficient B2B-opponent adjustment.

name: b2b_road_player_unders
thesis: Players on the second night of a back-to-back, playing away, see a 4-7% drop in points/rebounds/assists production vs their season averages, but books only adjust lines ~2%. The fatigue effect is strongest in the 4th quarter, meaning full-game overs are mispriced. Target player_points unders and player_points_rebounds_assists unders for starters logging 32+ min/game on B2B road legs.

name: b2b_road_prop_fade
thesis: Players on the second night of a back-to-back, playing away, see a 6-12% reduction in points scored vs their season average, but books only discount lines by 2-4%. The gap creates systematic over on player points props. Target high-usage guards (USG% > 25%) who rely on explosiveness rather than size/post play, as fatigue disproportionately affects perimeter creators.

name: b2b_second_night_player_unders
thesis: Star players (30+ min/game) on the second night of a back-to-back see a 6-12% reduction in points scored due to fatigue, but sportsbooks only discount their props by 2-4%. The under on player points for high-usage players (USG% > 25%) in B2B second nights should yield a persistent edge, especially when the B2B involves travel of 500+ miles between games.

name: b2b_second_night_under_props
thesis: Players on the second night of a back-to-back see statistically significant drops in points, assists, and PRA props due to fatigue, but books under-adjust lines by 2-4%. The edge is strongest for high-usage guards (30+ USG%) who rely on explosiveness rather than size. Target player_points unders when the player logged 34+ minutes in the prior night's game.

name: b2b_star_minutes_prop_over
thesis: On the second night of back-to-backs, books aggressively drop star player point totals anticipating rest or reduced minutes, but coaches increasingly play starters normal minutes in competitive games (seed races, rivalry). The under-adjustment creates value on the OVER for top-usage players (USG% > 28) when the team is within 4 games of a playoff seed. Test: compare implied prob of player points over vs actual hit rate on B2B nights for high-usage players on teams in playoff contention.

name: back_to_back_prop_deflation
thesis: Players on the second night of a back-to-back have their points/rebounds/assists props set lower by books, but the market overcorrects — actual performance drops less than the line adjustment, creating value on the OVER. Consensus devig across 3+ books will reveal systematic over-deflation of 3-5% on these props.

name: back_to_back_prop_deflation
thesis: Players on the second night of a back-to-back have their points/rebounds/assists props set too high by books that anchor on season averages. Consensus devig reveals persistent 4-7% edges on unders for starters playing 30+ min the prior night, particularly in the second half of the season when fatigue compounds.

name: blowout_minutes_rebound_unders
thesis: After a team wins or loses by 15+ points, starters' next-game rebounds props remain anchored to full-minute baselines, but coaches frequently adjust rotations—resting starters earlier in easy wins or going deeper into the bench after demoralizing losses. Rebounds props for starters on teams coming off blowouts (either side) show 3-5% edge on unders via consensus devig.

name: blowout_rest_spread_underreaction
thesis: Teams coming off a 20+ point win where starters rested the entire 4th quarter have a rest advantage the next game that books underweight. These teams cover the spread at 56%+ in their following game, especially on 0-1 days rest. Consensus devig will show the closing line underprices the rested team by 1-2 points.

name: closing_line_value_early_sharp
thesis: Lines that move 1.5+ points toward one side between opening and T-minus-4-hours consistently continue moving in the same direction into close. Early sharp action detected by comparing the opening line to the 4-hours-out line predicts closing line value. Betting the side the line is moving toward at T-4h captures 60%+ of remaining CLV, which correlates with long-term profitability. This is a meta-signal: don't model the game, model where the line is going.

name: closing_line_value_early_sharps
thesis: Lines that move 1.5+ points between opening and T-minus-4-hours in NBA spreads are driven by sharp early action. The opening line is mispriced and the closing line is efficient, so betting in the direction of early sharp movement at any price better than the eventual close captures persistent CLV. Track openers vs current lines at 4 hours pre-game; when movement exceeds 1.5 points, the current line still has residual edge because public money temporarily pushes back before close.

name: closing_line_value_stale_props
thesis: Player prop lines for non-marquee players (outside top-50 in usage rate) move significantly less than game lines between opening and tip-off. Books reprice spreads and totals aggressively as sharp money arrives, but player props for role players receive minimal attention and often reflect opening-night projections even after significant game-line movement. When a game total moves 3+ points, correlated player props for mid-tier players retain stale expected pace, creating systematic edge on overs when totals move up and unders when totals move down.

name: closing_line_value_stale_spread
thesis: When a spread opens and doesn't move for 4+ hours despite >60% of tickets on one side, the sharp money is on the non-public side. The book is holding the line as a trap. Betting the non-public side of stale lines where public % exceeds 60% yields 3-5% CLV and a 53-55% ATS win rate. This is strongest in nationally televised games where public betting volume is highest.

name: closing_line_value_totals_overreaction
thesis: When NBA game totals move 3+ points from open to 2 hours before tip (sharp action driving the move), the market overshoots by 0.8-1.2 points on average — the CLV reversal effect. The opening line anchored by overnight models is closer to true probability than the panic-driven late move. Fading large total movements (betting the opposite direction of the move at the moved line) yields +EV at the inflated number. Test: track games where total moves >= 3 points pre-tip, bet against the move direction, measure ROI vs closing line.

name: cross_country_early_game_1h_spread
thesis: Teams traveling 1,500+ miles for games starting before 8pm ET show a -1.3 ATS differential in the first half compared to their full-game ATS rate. Circadian disruption and travel fatigue manifest disproportionately early in the game. First-half spreads are typically set at ~51% of the full-game spread, but the actual first-half performance gap for long-haul travelers is closer to 58% of the full-game margin. Target: fading the traveler on 1H spreads in cross-country early-tip spots.

name: cross_country_travel_spread
thesis: NBA teams traveling 1,500+ miles for a game with no rest day underperform ATS by 1.5-2.5 points relative to their baseline, and this effect is not fully priced into spreads. The effect is strongest for westbound travel (losing hours) and for teams playing their 3rd game in 4 nights. Books partially adjust for back-to-backs but under-weight the compounding of distance + schedule density. Target the opponent spread or the traveling team's under on totals.

name: elite_positional_defense_points_under
thesis: Player points props are set primarily on the player's season averages with insufficient adjustment for the specific defensive matchup. When a primary scorer faces a top-5 ranked positional defense (e.g., wing scorer vs elite perimeter D, or center vs top interior D), the expected scoring suppression is 2-4 points beyond what the line reflects. The edge compounds when the defensive team also ranks top-10 in pace-adjusted defensive rating, reducing both efficiency and volume.

name: late_scratch_correlated_prop_lag
thesis: When an NBA starter is ruled out within 2 hours of tip-off, books reprice the absent player's props but under-adjust correlated teammates. The replacement starter and primary ball-handler see usage spikes that aren't fully priced into their props for 30-90 minutes after the announcement. Target overs on the highest-usage remaining teammate in the affected position cluster (e.g., PG assists when a secondary playmaker sits, C rebounds when PF is out).

name: late_sharp_movement_clv_signal
thesis: When a player prop line moves 0.5+ points in the final 3 hours before tip-off with no corresponding injury news, the move is driven by sharp syndicate action and the post-move line carries positive CLV 60%+ of the time. Betting the direction of the move at the new line still captures residual edge because DraftKings adjusts slower than Pinnacle/Circa. This is not speed-dependent arb — the edge persists for 30-60 minutes after the initial move.

name: load_management_return_pra_over
thesis: When a star player (top-40 usage rate) returns from a scheduled rest day (not injury), books anchor their prop lines conservatively to season averages or slightly below. However, these players are fresher than baseline and typically motivated to re-establish rhythm, producing above-average stat lines. Historical data shows ~60% over-hit rate on PRA in load management return games. The edge is strongest when the team lost during the rest game, adding a motivational catalyst.

name: nba_division_familiarity_total_under
thesis: Intra-division NBA matchups (teams playing each other 4x/season) produce systematically lower-scoring games than the posted total reflects, especially in the 3rd and 4th meetings of the season. Defensive familiarity with opponent tendencies, play calls, and personnel reduces offensive efficiency by 1-3 points per 100 possessions compared to non-division games. Books price totals using team-level offensive/defensive ratings without adequately weighting the familiarity discount. Target game total unders in division matchups from January onward.

name: pace_mismatch_total_mispricing
thesis: When a top-5 pace team faces a bottom-5 pace team, books anchor game totals closer to the average of both teams' implied totals. In reality, the fast team's possessions dominate the tempo — actual totals land 2-3 points higher than the posted line. The OVER is systematically underpriced in these matchups.

name: pace_mismatch_totals
thesis: When a top-5 pace team faces a bottom-5 pace team, books split the difference on game totals but historically the slower team's defensive identity dominates. Consensus devig across 3+ books should surface unders at 3-5% edge because markets overweight the fast team's offensive ceiling.

name: public_sharp_divergence_closing_line
thesis: When public betting percentage (>65% of tickets) favors one side but the line moves against the public (reverse line movement indicating sharp money), the sharp side covers at a 56-60% rate. This signal is strongest 2-6 hours before tip when sharp money arrives but books haven't fully adjusted. Player three-point props are particularly exploitable in this window because they receive less sharp attention and slower line corrections than spreads/totals.

name: public_sharp_divergence_threes
thesis: When public betting percentage on a player threes over is above 70% but the line has not moved or has moved down, sharp money is signaling the under. In these spots, the three-point prop under hits at 58%+ against the implied probability. Books hold the line to balance liability rather than reflecting true probability, creating a persistent edge on the under. Target: player threes unders where public % is 70%+ over but line is flat or dropping.

name: ref_crew_three_point_variance
thesis: Certain referee crews call significantly fewer fouls on perimeter play (bottom quartile in 3pt shooting fouls called per game), which increases three-point attempt volume by 5-8% as players settle for jumpers instead of driving. On nights with these crews, player threes overs for high-volume shooters (7+ 3PA/game) hit at 56-59% vs the implied 50%. The edge persists because ref assignments are published ~9am ET but books don't adjust props until closer to tip.

name: referee_crew_foul_tendency
thesis: NBA referee crews have persistent, measurable tendencies in foul calling rates. Games officiated by high-whistle crews see inflated free throw attempts, creating systematic mispricing on player points overs. By identifying crew assignments (typically released ~9am ET game day) and comparing crew-specific foul rates to the league mean, we can exploit the lag before books adjust lines. Target players with high FT rates (>5 FTA/game) in games with top-quartile whistle crews.

name: referee_crew_over_foul_props
thesis: Certain referee crews consistently call 8-12% more personal fouls per game than league average, directly inflating free throw attempts and player point totals. When a high-whistle crew (top quartile foul rate over last 30 games) is assigned, player points overs for high free-throw-rate players (8+ FTA/game) have positive expected value because books set lines based on season averages, not crew-adjusted projections.

name: referee_crew_three_point_foul_rate
thesis: Specific NBA referee crews call three-point shooting fouls at rates 30-50% above league average, inflating scoring opportunities for high-volume three-point shooters. When a top-10 volume 3PT shooter plays in a game with a high-foul-rate crew, their points prop has a systematic under-price because books don't adjust for ref assignment (announced ~9am ET day-of). The edge window is ref announcement to tip-off (~8 hours).

name: referee_crew_total_adjustment
thesis: NBA referee crew assignments are published ~9am ET on game day. Crews in the top quartile of fouls-per-game called show a +4.2 point average total deviation vs closing line over the last 3 seasons. Books do not reprice totals based on crew assignment until late afternoon sharp action forces it. Overs on game totals become +EV immediately after crew announcement for high-whistle crews, with the edge decaying by ~5pm ET as sharps correct the line.

name: referee_crew_total_bias
thesis: NBA referee crews show persistent, measurable tendencies in foul calling rates that directly impact game totals. Crews in the top quartile of fouls-per-game (historically 2+ fouls/game above league average) inflate totals by 4-6 points through free throw volume. When a high-whistle crew is assigned and the market total doesn't adjust (ref assignments posted ~9am ET, lines often static until noon), the over carries a consistent edge of 3-5%.

name: referee_crew_total_bias
thesis: NBA referee crews have persistent, measurable tendencies in foul calling rates that shift game totals by 3-5 points. Crews with top-quartile foul rates generate 6+ additional free throw attempts per game vs bottom-quartile crews, but books set totals using team-level models that treat officiating as noise. Once crew assignments are published (typically 9am ET game day), totals can be re-priced using crew-specific foul rate priors to find systematic over/under edges.

name: referee_foul_rate_overs
thesis: Certain NBA referee crews call 15-20% more personal fouls per game than league average. When high-whistle crews officiate, free throw attempt volume rises and game pace slows but scoring stays elevated due to FT volume. Player points overs for high-usage stars are mispriced by 2-4% in games officiated by top-quartile foul-calling crews because books set lines based on season averages, not crew-adjusted projections.

name: referee_foul_tendency_points_overs
thesis: Players with high free-throw rates (top-20% FTA/game) see inflated scoring when assigned referee crews that historically call 10%+ more personal fouls per game than league average. Books price player points props off season averages without adjusting for ref crew assignment, creating systematic over-pricing of unders for high-FTA players in these games.

name: referee_foul_tendency_totals
thesis: NBA ref crew assignments are published 1-2 hours before tip. Crews in the top quartile of fouls-per-game (historically) push game totals Over because more free throws inflate scoring. Books set totals before crew announcement and don't fully re-adjust, creating 2-4% Over edge on totals when a high-foul crew is assigned and the line doesn't move post-announcement.

name: rest_advantage_spread_home
thesis: Home teams with 2+ days rest facing opponents on 0-1 days rest cover the spread at 55-57% historically, but the market only prices ~1.5 points of rest advantage when the true value is closer to 2.5-3 points. The edge compounds when the rested home team is also in a playoff race (clinch number <= 5 games) as motivation amplifies the physical advantage. Target home spread when rest differential is 2+ days.

name: rest_advantage_three_pointers
thesis: Teams with 3+ days rest show a statistically significant increase in three-point shooting percentage (1.5-2.5% above season avg) in the first half, as fresh legs improve shot mechanics. Player threes overs for high-volume shooters (6+ 3PA/game) on well-rested teams are underpriced. The effect decays by the second half as game fatigue normalizes, but the full-game line is still mispriced because books weight season averages too heavily.

name: rest_disparity_ats
thesis: When one team has 3+ days of rest and their opponent is on 1 or fewer days rest, the rested team outperforms the spread by 1.5-2.5 points on average. Books partially adjust but the market underprices rest differentials of 2+ days, particularly when the fatigued team is also on the road. Target the rested team ATS when rest differential >= 2 days.

name: rest_disparity_late_spread
thesis: When rest differential is >= 2 days (e.g., team A has 3+ days off, team B on 0-1 days rest), the rested team outperforms the spread by 1.5-2.5 points on average, but this edge is largest when the line opens 12+ hours before tip and the rested team is a small underdog or pick'em (+1 to -3). Books partially price rest but underweight it for non-favorites. Test: track ATS performance segmented by rest differential and opening line range.

name: rest_disparity_spread_advantage
thesis: When one team has 3+ days of rest and their opponent is on 0-1 days rest (back-to-back or no rest day), the rested team outperforms the spread by 2.5-4 points on average. Books partially price rest but underweight the compounding effect of extreme rest disparities (3+ day gap). This edge is strongest in the second half and for teams ranked bottom-10 in depth (bench minutes), where fatigue disproportionately impacts the short-rested team's rotation.

name: rest_disparity_spread_overreaction
thesis: When a team with 3+ days rest faces an opponent on the second night of a back-to-back, the spread adjusts by roughly 1.5-2 points, but the empirical rest advantage is only 0.7-1.0 points ATS. The public overweights rest narratives, creating value on the fatigued team's spread. This effect is strongest when the rested team is already favored at home, doubling the public bias.

name: revenge_game_assist_boost
thesis: Players facing their former team for the first or second time post-trade show a statistically significant assists boost (+1.2-2.0 above season avg) rather than the commonly assumed points boost. The emotional motivation manifests as over-passing to prove they elevate teammates, not hero-ball. Books price points props tighter on revenge games but leave assists props at baseline, creating 4-7% edge on assists overs.

name: revenge_game_assist_inflation
thesis: Primary playmakers (top-2 assist leaders on team) facing their former team within 18 months of being traded show a statistically significant increase in assists (~1.5 above prop line) due to heightened aggression and usage rate. Books price player assist props off rolling averages but don't systematically identify and adjust for revenge-game usage spikes. The effect is strongest in the first matchup post-trade and decays by the third meeting.

name: revenge_game_player_threes
thesis: Players facing their former team within 2 seasons of being traded or leaving in free agency attempt and make more three-pointers than their season average, driven by elevated usage and adrenaline. Books set player_threes lines based on rolling averages and do not adjust for revenge-game motivation. Target overs on player_threes for primary scorers facing former teams, especially in the first matchup of the season.

name: revenge_game_prop_inflation
thesis: When a player faces their former team for the first or second time post-trade, public money inflates their player prop lines (especially points) by 1.5-3 points beyond what their recent form justifies. The 'revenge narrative' creates a systematic over on player_points lines. Fading the narrative — taking the under on the revenge player's points — should hit at 55%+ against consensus-devigged fair value.

name: revenge_game_threes_volume
thesis: Players facing their former team within 12 months of being traded attempt 15-25% more three-pointers than their season average due to heightened aggression and prove-it motivation. Books don't adjust three-point prop lines for revenge game context, creating 3-5% edge on player threes overs for recently traded players in their first 1-2 matchups against their old team.

name: revenge_game_usage_spike
thesis: NBA players facing their former team within the first 2 seasons after a trade or free agency departure show a statistically significant usage rate increase (+2-4% USG) driven by motivation and coach scheming. This usage spike translates to higher-than-normal scoring attempts, making player points overs +EV when the line is set based on season averages. The effect is strongest for players who were traded (not mutual departure) and for nationally televised games. Filter for players averaging 15+ PPG to avoid low-volume noise.

name: revenge_game_usage_spike
thesis: Players facing their former team within the first 2 matchups post-trade or free-agency departure show a statistically significant usage rate spike (1.5-3% above season average), translating to elevated points output. Books price props off season averages and don't model motivational factors. Points Overs for these players are +EV by 2-4% when consensus devig confirms the edge.

name: road_ft_suppression_points_under
thesis: Road players who rely heavily on free throws (top-quartile FTA/game) see measurable FT% drops in hostile road environments due to crowd noise. Books set player points props using season-average FT%, not split-adjusted rates. For players averaging 7+ FTA/game, the road FT% penalty (~2-4%) translates to 0.5-1.0 expected points below the posted line. Target points unders for high-FTA road players, especially in arenas with documented loud environments.

name: road_trip_leg3_rebound_collapse
thesis: Teams on the third or later leg of a road trip show a measurable decline in defensive rebounding rate (approximately 2-3% drop vs home baseline), driven by cumulative travel fatigue reducing box-out effort and second-jump explosiveness. Opposing centers and power forwards see inflated rebound totals in these spots, but books price player rebounds using rolling averages that don't isolate opponent road-trip depth as a factor. The edge is strongest for high-motor bigs facing a team on game 3+ of a road swing.

name: road_trip_three_point_decay
thesis: Teams on road trips of 4+ consecutive away games show a statistically significant decline in 3PT% (1.5-3% drop) by games 4-5 of the trip due to fatigue, unfamiliar rims, and disrupted routines. Books set player threes lines off rolling averages that include home games, creating systematic over-pricing. Test: compare player threes OVER hit rate for perimeter players (3PA > 5/game) during extended road trips vs their season baseline.

name: schedule_compression_3in4
thesis: Teams playing their 3rd game in 4 nights experience cumulative fatigue beyond what back-to-back adjustments capture. Player props for points_rebounds_assists are systematically set too high because books apply a single B2B discount but not a compounding fatigue factor. Unders on starters logging 32+ min/game are +EV by 3-5% in these spots.

name: schedule_density_pra_unders
thesis: Players on teams playing 4+ games within a 7-day window show measurable decline in combined PRA output (2-4% below season average) by game 4, even when not on a strict back-to-back. Books adjust for B2B but fail to price cumulative fatigue from schedule density. The effect is strongest for high-usage players (usage rate > 25%) aged 30+ who play 34+ minutes per game.

name: schedule_density_rebounds
thesis: When a team plays 4 games in 6 nights (beyond simple back-to-back), cumulative fatigue disproportionately affects perimeter players' rebounding effort while big men maintain theirs. Books price rebound props off rolling averages that don't weight schedule density. Center/PF rebound overs and guard rebound unders are mispriced by 3-6% in high-density schedule spots.

name: sharp_steam_move_follower
thesis: When 3+ tracked sharp books move a player prop line in the same direction within a 90-minute window while the target book (DraftKings) has not yet adjusted, this 'steam move' signal predicts closing line movement in that direction 68%+ of the time. The edge is largest in the first 30 minutes after the consensus shift and decays as books synchronize. Focus on player points, rebounds, and assists props where the stale line shows 3%+ deviation from the new sharp consensus.

name: three_point_regression_after_cold_streak
thesis: When a player who averages 35%+ from three on 5+ attempts per game has shot below 25% over their last 3 games, books lower their threes prop. Mean reversion is stronger than the market prices — the OVER on player threes hits at 55%+ in these spots, creating a devig edge of 4%+ vs consensus.

name: three_point_regression_bounce
thesis: Players who shot below 25% from three over their last 3 games (minimum 5 attempts per game) but have a season average above 36% are due for regression to the mean. Books anchor recent form too heavily on player threes props, creating value on the over. The edge is strongest when the player is at home (comfort, familiar rims) and the opposing team ranks bottom-10 in perimeter defense (opponent 3P% allowed).

name: three_point_regression_props
thesis: After a player hits 5+ threes in a game, books overcorrect their next-game threes prop upward by 0.5-1.0 makes. Three-point shooting is high-variance and mean-reverts sharply game-to-game. Unders on threes props after a hot shooting night should show 5%+ edge via consensus devig, especially for players with sub-37% season 3PT%.

name: timezone_cross_totals_depression
thesis: Teams crossing 2+ timezones for a road game (e.g., East Coast team playing Pacific, or vice versa) show depressed offensive efficiency in games starting before 8pm local time of the traveling team's origin city. Game totals should be lower than market-priced. Effect is ~2.5 points on the total, strongest when the traveling team arrived same-day. Books partially price travel but under-weight the circadian rhythm component specific to tip-off timing relative to origin timezone.

name: timezone_crossing_spread_fade
thesis: Teams crossing 2+ time zones for a road game (e.g., LAL at BOS, GSW at MIA) underperform against the spread by 1.5-2.5 points compared to baseline, particularly in early tip-off slots (before 2pm local time for the traveling team's home timezone). This fatigue signal compounds with short rest but is distinct from back-to-back effects — it persists even with 1 day rest if the travel distance is large enough.

name: west_to_east_early_game_unders
thesis: West Coast teams playing early-tip East Coast games (12:00-3:00 PM local, which is 9:00 AM-12:00 PM body clock time) show 4-7% depressed PRA totals due to circadian mismatch. This effect is strongest for guards and wing players who rely on reaction time and burst. Books set lines off season averages without adjusting for body-clock time, creating systematic mispricing on PRA unders.

name: west_to_east_early_tip_props
thesis: West Coast-based teams (Pacific timezone) playing road games with tip times before 7:30pm ET show reduced player output in points and assists, as circadian misalignment depresses performance. Books set prop lines based on season averages without sufficient road/timezone discount. Unders on top scorers are +EV by 2-3% in these spots.

name: NCAAB altitude visitor totals
thesis: Visiting teams playing at venues above 5000 feet elevation (Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, New Mexico, Air Force) see their team totals go under at a significantly higher rate than implied by the market. Reduced oxygen affects pace and shooting in the second half especially, but books set totals off full-season pace metrics. The edge is strongest when the visiting team played their previous game below 1000 feet elevation (maximum altitude differential).

name: NCAAB conference tournament fatigue totals
thesis: In NCAA conference tournament games where a team is playing its 3rd+ game in 3 days, total scoring drops significantly due to fatigue in shorter benches. Books set totals based on season averages and don't fully discount compressed schedules. Under is +EV by 3%+ when both teams have played 2+ games in the preceding 72 hours.

name: NCAAB conference tournament fatigue totals
thesis: Teams playing their 3rd+ game in 4 days during conference tournaments see depressed shooting efficiency due to fatigue, causing unders to hit at elevated rates. Books set totals based on season averages but underweight the cumulative fatigue of compressed tournament scheduling, especially for teams relying on short rotations (8 or fewer players averaging 10+ minutes).

name: NCAAB foul rate referee crew totals
thesis: Specific NCAAB referee crews call fouls at significantly different rates. When a high-whistle crew (top 20th percentile in fouls called per game) is assigned, books don't adjust totals upward enough to reflect the increased free throw attempts. Games officiated by high-foul crews exceed posted totals at a rate 3%+ above the implied Over probability. The edge persists because ref assignments are published 60-90 minutes before tip but books rarely re-price.

name: NCAAB free throw rate divergence player points
thesis: Player points overs on high-usage guards who draw fouls at above-average rates (top 20th percentile FTA/FGA) are underpriced when facing teams in the bottom quartile of personal foul rate. Books set player point lines primarily off scoring averages but underweight the FTA variance: a player averaging 18 PPG with 6 FTA/game facing a foul-prone defense can see 2-4 extra points from free throw volume alone. The edge is in the over on these player point props.

name: NCAAB mid-major spread overreaction
thesis: Mid-major conference teams (non-Power 6) that receive disproportionate public betting handle after a marquee upset win are overvalued in their next spread by 1.5-3 points. Books shade lines toward public money, but mid-majors that just pulled an upset often face letdown spots with inflated spreads. The edge is betting against the mid-major when public % exceeds 65% and the line has moved 1.5+ points from open toward them.

name: NCAAB seed-spread public bias
thesis: In NCAA tournament games, the public overvalues brand-name high seeds against mid-major low seeds, inflating the spread beyond fair value. When a mid-major 10-13 seed faces a power-conference 4-7 seed, the underdog spread is mispriced because books shade toward public money. The mid-major ATS cover rate exceeds implied probability by 4%+ in Round of 64 and Round of 32 matchups.

name: NCAAB tempo mismatch game totals
thesis: When a top-25 tempo team (possessions per 40 min) faces a bottom-25 tempo team in NCAAB, books anchor totals closer to the average of both teams' season totals. In reality, the slower team controls pace more effectively in college due to longer shot clock usage and less talent disparity. The Under hits at a higher rate than implied when the tempo differential exceeds 8 possessions per game.

name: NCAAB travel distance spread adjustment
thesis: NCAAB teams traveling 1000+ miles for away or neutral-site games underperform their spread at a higher rate than books imply, particularly when the game tips off before noon local time. College teams lack the charter-flight infrastructure of pro leagues, and early tip-offs compound the jet lag effect. Road/neutral teams in this situation fail to cover by 1.5+ points more than expected, creating +EV on the home/favored side.

name: NCAAB travel distance spread edge
thesis: Road teams traveling 1000+ miles for non-conference or tournament games underperform their spread by 1-2 points compared to short-travel road games (<300 miles). The effect compounds when the game tips before noon local time for the traveling team (early tips after long flights). Books partially price home court but underweight the specific fatigue cost of cross-country travel in the college game where teams lack charter flight infrastructure.

name: ncaab_3pt_variance_regression
thesis: Teams that shot 40%+ from three in their previous tournament game regress sharply (mean reversion to ~33-34%) in the next game, but books anchor spreads too heavily on the recent performance. Betting against teams whose spread tightened 2+ points after a hot-shooting win captures 3-5% edge on the opponent spread. Three-point shooting is the highest-variance stat in college basketball and books over-index on recency.

name: ncaab_altitude_travel_first_half_spread
thesis: Teams traveling from near sea level to venues above 4000ft (BYU, Colorado, Air Force, Wyoming, Utah, New Mexico) underperform first-half spreads by 1.5-2.5 points due to altitude-induced fatigue effects that dissipate by second half. First-half spread for the home altitude team is mispriced because full-game lines already partially account for this but H1 lines don't proportionally adjust.

name: ncaab_altitude_travel_spread
thesis: Teams traveling to tournament sites at 4000+ feet elevation (Denver, Salt Lake City, Boise) from sea-level home locations underperform their spread in the first game at altitude. The effect is 1.5-2.5 points of ATS value for the altitude-acclimated or shorter-travel team. Books do not adjust for altitude in neutral-site tournament pricing. This compounds with travel distance >1000 miles and timezone shifts of 2+ hours.

name: ncaab_altitude_travel_spread
thesis: Teams traveling to venues at 4000+ feet elevation (e.g., games in Denver, Salt Lake City, Albuquerque, Boise) underperform their spread in the first game at altitude, particularly when traveling from sea-level regions. The effect compounds with back-to-back travel days and is strongest in up-tempo games where cardio load is highest. Books do not systematically adjust for altitude in NCAAB lines. The home/host-site team at altitude covers at 56%+ against the spread.

name: ncaab_altitude_travel_totals
thesis: Games at high-altitude venues (5000+ feet: Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, Air Force, BYU) where the visiting team traveled from near sea level show suppressed scoring in the first half and depressed second-half shooting percentages. Books price full-game totals using season averages without adequately discounting the physiological impact of altitude on visiting teams unaccustomed to thin air. The effect is strongest for up-tempo teams that rely on fast-break scoring. Target: first-half and full-game unders.

name: ncaab_altitude_travel_totals
thesis: Games played at venues above 4500ft elevation (BYU, Colorado, Air Force, Utah, New Mexico, Wyoming) see unders hit at 56%+ when the visiting team traveled from a sub-1000ft home venue. Visiting teams shoot 2-4% worse from three in altitude games due to ball flight physics and fatigue compounding. Books price totals off season averages without adjusting for altitude-naive visitors.

name: ncaab_altitude_venue_over
thesis: NCAA Tournament games played at high-altitude venues (>4000ft — Denver, Salt Lake City, Boise) see the OVER hit at elevated rates when both teams are from low-altitude home courts. Decreased air density increases shooting accuracy (less ball drag, flatter arc) while fatigue effects are minimal in 40-minute games with TV timeouts. Books price totals off season averages played predominantly at low altitude, underweighting the shooting bump. Effect is 2-3 points on the total.

name: ncaab_altitude_venue_shooting
thesis: When NCAA tournament games are played at venues above 4500 feet elevation (Denver, Salt Lake City, Boise), teams based below 1000 feet elevation shoot worse from three-point range and game totals hit the under at elevated rates. The effect compounds when the low-altitude team has not played at elevation in the prior 30 days. Books do not adjust totals or player threes props for altitude despite measurable effects on ball flight and aerobic capacity.

name: ncaab_altitude_visitor_threes
thesis: Visiting teams playing at venues above 4500 feet elevation (Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, New Mexico, Air Force) show a measurable decline in three-point shooting percentage (~2-3pp) compared to their season average. Books do not adjust player three-point prop lines for altitude. The under on visitor player threes is systematically +EV at high-altitude venues, especially for teams based below 1000 feet.

name: ncaab_auto_bid_upset_moneyline
thesis: Small-conference automatic qualifiers (teams seeded 13-16 that won their conference tournament) offer positive expected value on the moneyline in first-round NCAA tournament games when the closing line implies <22% win probability. Books and the public systematically overweight seed number and conference prestige, but auto-bid teams are battle-tested from winning 3-4 elimination games in rapid succession. The combination of peak form, nothing-to-lose mentality, and public money inflating the favorite creates moneyline value. Historical upset rates for 12-16 seeds exceed implied probabilities by 3-6%.

name: ncaab_back_to_back_player_props
thesis: In conference tournaments and March Madness, star players (top 2 usage rate on team) playing their 3rd game in 5 days see a 12-18% drop in points scored relative to season average, yet player point props are discounted only 5-8% from season line. The under on points props for high-usage players in scheduling crunches yields 4-6% edge. Effect is strongest for players over 34% usage rate who cannot be load-managed in elimination settings.

name: ncaab_bubble_team_motivation_spread
thesis: Teams on the NCAA tournament bubble (projected as last four in / first four out) outperform the spread by 1.5-3 points in late-season games against opponents with locked seeding or no tournament aspirations. Books underweight motivation asymmetry in college basketball because roster-level effort variance is higher than in professional leagues. Bubble teams play with elimination urgency while locked-in opponents rest starters or experiment with rotations. This edge is strongest in the final 2 weeks of the regular season and in conference tournament early rounds.

name: ncaab_closing_line_value_early_round
thesis: NCAAB Tournament lines in rounds 1-2 move sharply toward the favorite between 48-12 hours before tip as public money floods in on name brands and higher seeds. Teams that open as 1-3 point underdogs but move to 3-5 point underdogs by close cover the closing spread at >57%. Grabbing the opening line on these underdogs and comparing to the consensus-devigged true probability at close reveals a persistent CLV edge of 2-4% that books give away through public-driven drift.

name: ncaab_closing_line_value_early_underdog_ml
thesis: NCAAB tournament underdog moneylines posted at market open (48+ hours pre-game) offer persistent closing line value of 3-6% when the underdog is seeded 8-12 and the line opens with implied probability under 35%. Early tournament lines are set conservatively by books with limited March-specific data, and sharp action compresses the line toward the underdog as game time approaches. Betting the underdog ML at open and tracking CLV confirms the edge is real, not noise.

name: ncaab_conf_tourney_loser_bounce
thesis: Teams that lost their conference tournament championship game and received an at-large NCAA Tournament bid outperform their spread in the first round by 2-3 points on average. The market overweights the recency of the conference final loss (narrative: 'they choked'), but these teams are typically elite and motivated. The edge is strongest for power-conference teams seeded 3-6.

name: ncaab_conference_rubber_match_overs
thesis: When two teams from the same conference meet for the 3rd time in a season (regular season twice, then conference or NCAA tournament), game totals hit the over at 56%+ because both coaching staffs have fully scouted each other's sets, leading to aggressive offensive adjustments and faster pace. Books set totals near the average of the first two meetings, but the third meeting consistently plays faster due to schematic familiarity reducing defensive hesitation and increasing transition opportunities.

name: ncaab_conference_tournament_fatigue
thesis: Teams playing their 3rd+ game in 4 days during conference tournaments see degraded shooting efficiency, particularly in second halves. Player prop unders on points and threes for high-usage guards become profitable as fatigue compounds and books anchor to season-long averages rather than adjusting for compressed schedules.

name: ncaab_conference_tournament_fatigue
thesis: Teams that played 4+ games in their conference tournament before entering the NCAA tournament show measurable fatigue effects in their first NCAA tournament game, particularly on the defensive end. This manifests as opponents exceeding their season scoring averages. Backing the opponent spread or the over in these spots yields a 3-5% edge because tournament fatigue is not priced into lines that rely on season-long metrics.

name: ncaab_conference_tournament_fatigue
thesis: Teams playing their 3rd+ game in 3-4 days during conference tournaments show degraded second-half shooting efficiency. Books don't adequately adjust spreads or totals for cumulative fatigue in compressed schedules. The under on team totals and the opponent spread become +EV when a team has played 48+ minutes in the prior 72 hours, especially for teams with 7-man rotations.

name: ncaab_conference_tourney_fatigue
thesis: Teams playing their 3rd game in 3 days during conference tournaments show degraded shooting efficiency, particularly in the second half. Books adjust spreads insufficiently for cumulative fatigue in mid-major conferences where depth is shallow. The under on team totals and the opponent spread become +EV when a team has played 2 games in the prior 48 hours.

name: ncaab_conference_tourney_fatigue_totals
thesis: Teams playing their 3rd+ game in 4 days during conference tournaments see inflated totals lines because books anchor to season averages, but shooting efficiency drops 3-5% due to fatigue accumulation. Unders on totals hit at elevated rates when both teams are on short rest in tournament settings.

name: ncaab_conference_tourney_fatigue_totals
thesis: In NCAA conference tournament games where at least one team is playing its 3rd game in 3 days, unders on team totals hit at a higher rate because fatigue degrades offensive efficiency (eFG%, turnover rate) more than books adjust for. Mid-major conferences with fewer rest days between games show the strongest effect.

name: ncaab_conference_tourney_fatigue_unders
thesis: Teams playing their 3rd or 4th game in 4 days during conference tournaments show statistically significant scoring drops. Player prop Overs are overpriced because books anchor to season averages rather than adjusting for accumulated fatigue, foul trouble accumulation, and shortened rotations in compressed schedules. Under on player points and PRA combos should yield +EV when a team has played 2+ games in the prior 72 hours.

name: ncaab_conference_tourney_fatigue_unders
thesis: In NCAA conference tournament games where at least one team is playing its 3rd game in 4 days, game totals are systematically overpriced. Books set lines based on season averages but fail to discount cumulative fatigue, shorter prep time, and tighter rotations typical of mid-major conference tournaments with compressed schedules. Target: game total unders when fatigue factor is present and consensus devig shows 3%+ edge.

name: ncaab_foul_prone_star_player_props
thesis: When a team's leading scorer has a season foul rate above 3.5 per game and faces a team ranked top-50 in free throw rate allowed (meaning they draw fouls aggressively / refs call tight), the player's points prop under hits at an elevated rate. Books set props off season averages but don't adequately discount for matchup-specific foul trouble risk that limits minutes. Edge is strongest in tournament/neutral-site games where refs trend tighter.

name: ncaab_free_throw_regression_tournament
thesis: NCAAB teams shooting >78% from the free throw line in regular season regress toward 72-73% in neutral-site tournament games due to crowd noise, pressure, and unfamiliar rims. Books price spreads using season-long FT%, creating an edge on unders and against teams whose win margin is FT-dependent. Teams whose scoring margin shrinks by 3+ points when FT% drops to league average are vulnerable.

name: ncaab_freshman_minutes_prop_leak
thesis: Freshman-heavy rotations (3+ freshmen averaging 20+ min) see player point props mispriced in March because books use season-long averages, but freshman scoring variance increases 15-20% under tournament pressure. Overs on the top freshman scorer and unders on the 2nd/3rd options create a correlated edge as shot distribution concentrates.

name: ncaab_freshman_minutes_prop_leak
thesis: Star freshmen on tournament teams see 10-15% more minutes in elimination games than their season average, but player point props are still anchored to regular-season per-game averages. This creates systematic under-pricing on points overs for high-usage freshmen (usage rate 25%+) in tournament games. The effect is amplified when the team's second option is a senior role player who defers in high-pressure spots.

name: ncaab_freshman_minutes_prop_unders
thesis: Freshman-heavy teams (40%+ of minutes played by freshmen) see individual player stat lines become more volatile and regression-prone in high-pressure tournament settings. Books set player prop lines anchored to regular season averages but freshmen experience sharper performance drops in first tournament exposure. Player points unders on freshmen in their first NCAA tournament game carry a measurable edge.

name: ncaab_freshman_pressure_unders
thesis: Tournament games where both teams rely heavily on freshmen (40%+ of minutes played by freshmen) go under the total at an elevated rate (~55%). First-year players in a single-elimination, neutral-site, nationally-televised environment see shooting efficiency drop 3-5% vs regular season. Books price totals off season-long offensive ratings without discounting for tournament pressure on inexperienced rosters.

name: ncaab_freshmen_usage_spike_unders
thesis: In NCAA tournament games where a team's leading scorer is a freshman or sophomore whose usage rate must increase 15%+ due to an injured or foul-prone upperclassman, that team's team total hits the under at 58%+. Young players facing elimination-pressure minutes against tournament-caliber defenses experience efficiency drops that books fail to price because they weight season-long stats. The edge is strongest when the usage spike is forced by injury news within 48 hours of tip.

name: ncaab_ft_rate_spread_edge
thesis: In NCAAB, free throw rate differential (FTA/FGA) between two teams is a stronger spread predictor than the market prices in. Teams in the top quartile of FT rate facing bottom-quartile FT rate teams cover spreads at 56%+ because college referees call more fouls than NBA refs, amplifying this advantage. The edge is largest when the high-FT-rate team is also the underdog, as the market underweights their ability to manufacture points from the line in tight games.

name: ncaab_geographic_proximity_r1
thesis: In NCAA tournament first and second round games, teams playing within 300 miles of their campus have a measurable home-court-like advantage that is underpriced by 1.5-2 points in the spread market. This effect compounds when the proximate team is a mid-major with a passionate local fanbase, as ticket allocation and travel ease create a pseudo-home environment. The edge is detectable via consensus devig showing the proximate team's implied probability lagging their true win rate in these spots.

name: ncaab_low_seed_totals_under
thesis: Tournament games between two teams seeded 9 or higher (mid-majors, lower seeds) systematically go under the posted total. Books set totals based on season-long offensive efficiency, but low-seed tournament teams play tighter, more deliberate basketball under elimination pressure. Pace drops 3-5% vs regular season, and unfamiliarity between non-conference opponents produces more half-court sets. The under hits at 55%+ in these matchups.

name: ncaab_low_tempo_under_mispricing
thesis: When two teams both ranked in the bottom quartile of adjusted tempo (sub-64 possessions per game) meet, books systematically set the total too high by 2-4 points. The compounding effect of two slow teams is non-linear — pace drops further than the average of their individual tempos because both teams succeed at dictating pace. The under is +EV when both teams are bottom-25% tempo and the total hasn't already been steamed down by sharps.

name: ncaab_low_tempo_underdog_spread
thesis: When a low-tempo team (sub-65 possessions per game) is an underdog of 4-10 points, they cover the spread at a significantly higher rate than implied by the line. Slow-paced teams compress variance and keep games close, but books anchor spreads on raw scoring differentials rather than per-possession efficiency gaps. Effect is strongest when the favorite is a top-25 tempo team forced to play at the underdog's pace.

name: ncaab_mid_major_closing_line_value
thesis: Mid-major conference games (outside Power 5) have thinner betting markets and less sharp action, causing lines to be set inefficiently and move slowly. When the devigged consensus from 3+ books diverges from DraftKings by 3%+ on mid-major spreads, the closing line correction is larger and slower than for high-profile games, creating a window of 2-6 hours pre-game where stale lines persist. Betting the consensus side on mid-major spreads when divergence exceeds threshold should capture closing line value.

name: ncaab_mid_major_closing_line_value
thesis: Mid-major conference tournament champions who earn auto-bids as 12-16 seeds show persistent closing line value (CLV) of +1.5 to +3 points in their first tournament game. Opening lines overreact to seed/conference prestige gap. Sharp money corrects toward the mid-major between open and tip, but the opening line still offers exploitable value if captured within 2 hours of posting. Track CLV to validate edge existence before live betting.

name: ncaab_mid_major_home_dog_ats
thesis: Mid-major conference home underdogs of 1-6 points in regular season games cover at a rate significantly above 50%. Public money disproportionately backs power conference brands and higher seeds, inflating lines against lesser-known programs playing in hostile home environments with unfamiliar travel for visitors. Small arenas with rabid fanbases and unique court dimensions amplify home court advantage beyond what books price. Target: ATS when mid-major home team is 1-6 point underdog.

name: ncaab_mid_major_spread_overreaction
thesis: When a mid-major (conference RPI 10+) upsets a power conference team, books over-adjust the mid-major's spread in their next game by 1.5-3 points due to public perception shift. Fading the mid-major (taking their opponent) in the game immediately following a marquee upset yields positive CLV.

name: ncaab_mid_major_totals_deflation
thesis: When a mid-major (conference rank 8+) faces a power conference team in the tournament, books systematically set totals 2-4 points too low. The public assumes blowout-slow-pace, but mid-majors that survive to later rounds play up-tempo to compensate for talent gaps. The under is overbet by the public, creating value on overs at consensus-devigged implied probabilities below 48%.

name: ncaab_mid_major_travel_spread
thesis: Mid-major conference teams traveling 1000+ miles for neutral-site or away tournament games underperform their spread at a higher rate than power conference teams making equivalent trips. Books price travel disruption uniformly but mid-majors have smaller rosters, fewer charter flights, and less institutional support for road logistics. Spread value exists fading traveling mid-majors in early tournament rounds.

name: ncaab_neutral_site_three_point_regression
thesis: Three-point shooting percentage regresses significantly at neutral-site tournament venues compared to home/away regular season games due to unfamiliar sight lines, depth perception, and crowd positioning. Books price player threes props based on season averages that include inflated home shooting splits. Players who derive a large share of their scoring from threes see the biggest regression at neutral sites, creating systematic unders value on player threes props in March Madness and conference tournament neutral-site games.

name: ncaab_public_bias_mid_seed_dog
thesis: In 5-vs-12 and 6-vs-11 NCAA Tournament matchups, when public betting exceeds 60% on the underdog (the popular upset pick), the favorite covers at a 57%+ rate. The 'everyone picks a 12-seed upset' narrative inflates the line toward the dog, creating value on the chalk. This is the inverse of sharp money — the public systematically over-bets mid-seed upsets because of bracket pool incentives, not edge.

name: ncaab_public_bias_tournament_spreads
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games, public money disproportionately backs higher-seeded (lower number) teams and brand-name programs, inflating their spread by 1-2 points beyond true probability. When a lower-seeded team (9-16 seed) faces a historically popular program and the consensus devig shows the spread is 2%+ wider than fair value, the lower seed ATS is +EV. This effect is strongest in Round of 64 and Round of 32 where casual bettors flood the market.

name: ncaab_public_blue_blood_fade
thesis: When public betting percentage exceeds 70% on traditional blue blood programs (Duke, Kentucky, Kansas, UNC, UCLA) as tournament favorites of -3 or more, the line is inflated by 1.5-2.5 points due to recreational money. Fading these teams against the spread yields positive CLV. Effect amplifies in nationally televised primetime slots where casual bettors concentrate.

name: ncaab_public_blue_blood_spread_inflation
thesis: Marquee NCAAB programs (Duke, Kentucky, Kansas, UNC, UCLA, etc.) in nationally televised tournament games receive disproportionate public money, inflating their spread by 1-2 points beyond true probability. Fading these teams against the spread when consensus devig shows edge >= 3% yields positive CLV. Effect is strongest in Round of 64 and Round of 32 where casual bettors dominate handle.

name: ncaab_public_darling_fade_march
thesis: During March Madness, teams seeded 5-8 that received disproportionate public betting handle (>65% of tickets) as favorites against 9-12 seeds are overvalued. The public overweights brand-name programs and recent TV exposure. Fading these public darlings on the spread yields closing line value because sharp money arrives late to correct the line, creating a window 12-4 hours before tip where the dog side is +EV.

name: ncaab_public_favorite_ats_fade
thesis: When a Power 6 conference team is favored by 5+ points against a mid-major in the NCAA Tournament Round of 64 or 32, and public betting percentage exceeds 70% on the favorite, the underdog covers ATS at 55%+ rate. Casual March bettors overweight brand-name programs, inflating lines beyond true probability. The edge is strongest when the mid-major ranks top-50 in KenPom adjusted efficiency margin but has low national TV exposure.

name: ncaab_public_hype_fade_march
thesis: In March Madness, teams receiving 70%+ of public spread bets (per consensus public betting percentages) that are also 7+ point favorites fail to cover at a significantly higher rate than implied. Casual bettor influx during the tournament inflates lines on popular brands (Duke, Kansas, UNC) beyond true probability. Fading heavy public sides on large favorites yields persistent CLV.

name: ncaab_public_money_fade_large_spreads
thesis: When a team seeded 1-4 is favored by 12+ points in the tournament, public money concentrates heavily on the favorite (70%+ of bets), but the underdog covers the spread at 54%+ historically. Books shade lines 1-2 points toward the public favorite, creating systematic value on large underdogs. The effect is strongest in the Round of 64 where casual bettors flood the market and name recognition drives one-sided action.

name: ncaab_public_overbet_upset_moneyline
thesis: In March Madness first-round games where the favorite receives >75% of public moneyline handle but sharp reverse line movement moves the underdog's line down (or holds steady despite public action), the underdog moneyline has positive expected value. Books shade toward public money on marquee matchups, and sharp money on the other side signals genuine disagreement with the market. 12-over-5 and 11-over-6 seeds show the strongest historical signal in this pattern.

name: ncaab_public_seed_bias_spreads
thesis: In NCAA tournament games, public money disproportionately backs trendy upset seeds (11, 12, 13) against 4-6 seeds, inflating the moneyline and compressing the spread for the lower seed. When public betting exceeds 60% on the underdog in these matchups, the favorite covers at an elevated rate because the line has moved away from true value. This is strongest in Round 1 where casual March Madness bettors flood the market.

name: ncaab_public_seed_bias_spreads
thesis: In NCAA tournament matchups between a top-4 seed and a 5-12 seed, the lower seed covers the spread at a rate exceeding 54% when consensus opening spread is 5+ points. Casual public money inflates brand-name program lines, and books shade toward the popular side. The inefficiency is strongest in the Round of 32 and Sweet 16 where public attention peaks but informational edges for sharps on mid-majors persist. Closing line movement toward the underdog confirms sharp disagreement.

name: ncaab_public_seed_bias_totals
thesis: NCAA Tournament games featuring a 1-4 seed vs a 12-16 seed see inflated totals due to public expectation of blowouts. In reality, lower seeds frequently slow pace to stay competitive, compressing possessions. Unders in these matchups hit at >54% when the total is set above the lower-seeded team's season-average pace-adjusted total. The edge is strongest in rounds 1-2 where public handle is heaviest.

name: ncaab_referee_crew_foul_totals
thesis: NCAA referee crew assignments are published pre-game but rarely priced into totals or spreads. Certain referee crews call 15-20% more fouls per game than average, directly inflating free throw attempts and pace. When a high-whistle crew is assigned to a game between two physical, low-tempo teams, the game total is systematically underpriced because the additional stoppages and free throws add 4-8 points above the baseline. Target: game total overs when high-foul referee crew is assigned to physical matchups.

name: ncaab_rematch_over_adjustment
thesis: When conference rivals meet for the 2nd or 3rd time in a season, books overcorrect totals based on the previous meeting's score. If Game 1 was a blowout or unusually low-scoring, Game 2 totals are shaded too far in the opposite direction due to mean-reversion overcompensation. When the rematch total diverges 3%+ from devigged consensus and the prior meeting's total was 10+ points from the season average for both teams, the consensus side on totals is +EV.

name: ncaab_rest_advantage_tournament_bracket
thesis: In tournament settings where one team had an extra rest day (e.g., bye round, earlier tip time in prior round by 24+ hours), the rested team's player prop totals for points and assists are underpriced. Books adjust spreads for rest but under-adjust individual player props, especially for guards who drive tempo. The edge is strongest when the fatigued team played overtime or a game exceeding 2.5 hours in their prior round.

name: ncaab_revenge_game_spread_overreaction
thesis: When a team lost to an in-conference opponent by 10+ points earlier in the season and is now a home underdog or small favorite in the rematch, the market underprices the motivational edge. These revenge spots show a +2.1 ATS lean historically because coaches scheme specifically for rematches and players elevate intensity. The spread on the revenge team is +EV when the line hasn't moved more than 1 point from open.

name: ncaab_seed_spread_overreaction
thesis: In NCAA tournament matchups where the seed differential is 5+, books overprice the favorite spread due to public money flooding name-brand programs. Mid-major and lower-seeded teams with top-50 defensive efficiency cover at a higher rate than implied by consensus lines. The edge is largest in rounds 1-2 where casual bettors drive the handle.

name: ncaab_short_rest_tournament_total_unders
thesis: Tournament games where at least one team played the previous day (0-1 rest days) see total scoring 3-5 points below the posted total. Books adjust rest in NBA pricing but underweight it in NCAAB tournaments where young players with shorter benches fatigue faster. This effect compounds when both teams are on short rest. Conference tournament games on consecutive days and NCAA tournament Thursday-Saturday sequences are the primary targets. The effect is strongest in second halves where fatigue manifests as lower shooting efficiency and higher turnover rates.

name: ncaab_star_player_over_props_elimination
thesis: In NCAA tournament elimination games (Round of 64, Round of 32), the leading scorer on each team exceeds their regular-season points prop at an elevated rate. Books price player props off season averages, but tournament minutes increase 2-4 minutes for stars as coaches shorten rotations. Combined with higher usage rates in win-or-go-home contexts, star players in the 18-22 PPG range consistently exceed their posted lines by 2+ points.

name: ncaab_star_player_prop_tournament_usage_spike
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games, the top scorer on each team sees a 3-8% usage rate increase compared to regular season as coaches shorten rotations and ride their best players in elimination games. Player point props set off regular-season averages systematically undershoot tournament performance for primary options averaging 16+ PPG. The OVER on points for the #1 scoring option hits at 57%+ when their team's bench minutes dropped >15% in conference tournament play.

name: ncaab_star_player_prop_tournament_variance
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games, star players (top scorer on their team, averaging 18+ PPG) on favored teams (-5 or more) see their points props set too high. Books set lines based on season averages, but blowouts lead to reduced 2nd-half minutes, and tournament defensive intensity compresses usage. Points unders for these players hit >56% when their team is favored by 7+. Conversely, star players on underdog teams in close-line games (+1 to +5) exceed their props at >55% due to increased usage in must-win scenarios.

name: ncaab_star_player_props_low_visibility
thesis: Player point props for high-usage NCAAB stars (usage rate >= 28%) on mid-major or low-major teams are systematically mispriced because books set these lines with wider margins and less sharp money corrects them. When consensus devig across 3+ books shows >= 4% edge on the over for a player averaging 18+ PPG with usage >= 28%, the inefficiency persists through tipoff because the market lacks liquidity to correct it.

name: ncaab_star_player_props_post_blowout
thesis: Star players (top usage rate on team) have suppressed stat lines in games immediately following a blowout loss (15+ points), as coaches adjust game plans, tighten rotations, and shift to more conservative offensive schemes. Books anchor prop lines to rolling averages that include normal variance but don't discount the tactical reset after embarrassing losses. Target: player points unders for high-usage players in the game after a blowout loss.

name: ncaab_star_player_tournament_pra_overs
thesis: Top-usage players (usage rate >28%) on teams expected to be competitive (spread within 8 points) see inflated minutes and touches in NCAA tournament games compared to regular season averages, creating overs value on PRA props. Tournament games feature tighter rotations as coaches shorten benches to 7-8 players, and star players see 2-4 extra minutes per game. Books price PRA props off season averages that include blowout minutes reductions and mid-season rest games. The combination of higher minutes, higher stakes possessions, and increased free throw attempts from aggressive play inflates PRA by 2-4 points above the season mean.

name: ncaab_tempo_mismatch_over
thesis: When a top-30 tempo team (adjusted possessions per 40 min) faces a bottom-100 tempo team in the tournament, the total goes over at an elevated rate. Books average the two tempos, but empirically the faster team dictates pace more often than the slower team controls it, especially in early rounds where the slower team lacks film on the opponent's transition game. The over hits at 56%+ when the tempo differential exceeds 6 possessions per game.

name: ncaab_tempo_mismatch_total
thesis: When two teams with a tempo differential exceeding 8 possessions per game meet, books anchor game totals too heavily toward the average of both teams' season averages. In practice, the slower team controls pace more reliably in NCAAB than NBA due to longer shot clocks relative to game flow and coaching emphasis on half-court sets. Unders hit at 55%+ when the slower team is also the favorite (controlling possession more often).

name: ncaab_tempo_mismatch_totals
thesis: When a top-30 tempo team faces a bottom-30 tempo team, the game total is systematically mispriced. Books split the difference but the slower team's pace control dominates in college basketball where shot clock management and half-court sets compress possessions. Unders hit at elevated rates in these extreme tempo mismatches, especially when the slow team is favored or a small underdog.

name: ncaab_tempo_mismatch_totals
thesis: When a top-30 pace team faces a bottom-30 pace team in NCAAB, the total is systematically mispriced. Books anchor to an average of the two tempos, but the slower team controls pace ~60% of possessions. Unders hit at 56%+ in these matchups, with the edge increasing when the slow team is the underdog (books assume the favorite dictates tempo).

name: ncaab_tempo_mismatch_totals
thesis: When two NCAAB teams with pace differential >= 8 possessions per game meet, the total is mispriced because books anchor to season averages rather than modeling the slower team's ability to control tempo. Unders hit at a higher rate when the slower team is disciplined defensively (adj defensive efficiency top 50 per KenPom) and the faster team lacks half-court offense (assist rate below 50%). Edge persists because NCAAB pace data is noisier and less incorporated into lines than NBA.

name: ncaab_tempo_mismatch_under
thesis: When a bottom-quartile tempo team (sub-64 possessions/game) faces a top-quartile tempo team (68+ possessions/game), the game total goes UNDER at a 56%+ rate against the closing line. Books split the difference on pace, but the slower team controls tempo more reliably in college due to the 30-second shot clock and coaching discipline. The under is sharpest when the slow team is favored or a small underdog (<4 pts).

name: ncaab_tempo_mismatch_unders
thesis: When a top-40 tempo team (possessions per game) faces a bottom-40 tempo team in NCAAB, the slower team controls pace disproportionately. Totals markets are set closer to the average of the two tempos, but empirically the game plays closer to the slow team's pace. Unders hit at 55%+ in these mismatches, creating a persistent pre-game edge on totals.

name: ncaab_thin_bench_b2b_fatigue
thesis: NCAAB teams with rotation depth <= 7 players (measured by players averaging 15+ minutes) underperform the spread when playing their 3rd game in 4 days during conference tournaments. Thin benches accumulate fatigue faster than books adjust for, especially mid-majors where depth data is less tracked by the market.

name: ncaab_three_point_regression_props
thesis: Player three-point props are mispriced following a hot shooting game (4+ threes made in prior game). Books and public overweight recency, but three-point shooting regresses sharply to season mean in college due to higher variance with younger shooters and varied defensive schemes. The under on player threes is +EV when a player exceeded their season average by 2+ threes in their most recent game, particularly in tournament play where defensive scouting intensifies between rounds.

name: ncaab_three_point_regression_totals
thesis: When a team shoots 40%+ from three in back-to-back games, books overweight the hot shooting in the next game's total. NCAA three-point shooting regresses harder than NBA due to smaller sample sizes and wider talent variance. Unders on games where one or both teams had consecutive 40%+ three-point games yield 3-6% edge as totals are inflated by 2-4 points.

name: ncaab_timezone_travel_spread
thesis: Teams traveling 2+ time zones for tournament site games underperform spreads by 1-2 points in their first game at that site, particularly in early tip-off slots (before 2pm local). Books price neutral-site games as truly neutral but ignore circadian disruption. West Coast teams playing East Coast morning tips and vice versa show the strongest effect. The edge disappears by the second game at the same site as teams acclimate.

name: ncaab_tournament_fatigue_unders
thesis: In NCAA tournament games where at least one team is playing its 3rd game in 5 days (conference tournament into March Madness, or deep tournament runs), game totals hit the under at a significantly higher rate. Fatigued legs reduce shooting efficiency and pace, but books anchor totals to season averages that don't account for compressed scheduling. Edge is largest when both teams are in this situation.

name: ncaab_tournament_public_bias_underdog
thesis: In NCAA tournament games where the lower-seeded team (underdog) has a closing spread of +4 to +10, public betting percentages heavily favor the higher-seeded (name brand) team, creating inflated lines. Mid-major and low-profile programs that earned their seed through strong conference play are systematically undervalued by recreational bettors, leading to positive closing line value on the underdog spread.

name: ncaab_tournament_rest_disparity
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games where one team had 2+ fewer rest days than their opponent (e.g., play-in winners vs teams with a bye), the rested team covers the spread at a rate exceeding implied probability by 4-6%. Books underweight cumulative fatigue and travel in 48-hour turnarounds because public money chases Cinderella narratives on the short-rest team.

name: ncaab_tournament_rest_disparity
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games where one team had 2+ fewer rest days than their opponent (e.g., play-in winners vs teams with byes, or teams from grueling conference tournament runs), the rested team covers the spread at a rate >55%. Books underweight cumulative fatigue in single-elimination settings because they anchor on season-long metrics rather than recency-weighted conditioning. Target the rested side when the spread implies <52% implied probability for them.

name: ncaab_tournament_rest_disparity
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games where one team had 3+ days rest and the opponent had 2 or fewer days rest, the rested team outperforms the spread by 1.5-3 points. Tournament scheduling creates asymmetric rest that books underweight because seed-based priors dominate their lines. This is strongest in Sweet 16 and Elite 8 rounds where fatigue compounds from earlier rounds.

name: ncaab_tournament_rest_disparity_totals
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games where one team had 2+ fewer days of rest than their opponent (e.g., play-in winners vs teams with byes, or compressed bracket scheduling), the total goes UNDER at a statistically significant rate. Fatigued teams shoot worse from three (2-4% drop in 3PT%) and commit more turnovers, compressing scoring output. Books set totals based on season averages and don't fully discount acute fatigue in single-elimination contexts.

name: ncaab_tournament_rest_edge
thesis: In NCAA Tournament games, teams with 2+ days rest facing teams with 1 day rest (common in bracket scheduling mismatches) outperform the spread by 1.5-3 points. Books underweight rest differential in tournament settings because they anchor on seed/ranking. This edge is strongest in Round of 32 and Sweet 16 where rest asymmetry is most common.

name: ncaab_tournament_rest_edge
thesis: In NCAA tournament games, teams with 2+ days rest facing teams that played the prior day cover the spread at a significantly higher rate. The combination of physical recovery, extra preparation time, and film study creates a measurable edge that books underweight because they anchor on seed lines and public perception rather than scheduling advantage. Target spreads where the rested team is getting points or is a small favorite.

name: ncaab_travel_distance_early_tipoff
thesis: NCAAB teams traveling 1000+ miles to a neutral-site tournament venue and tipping off before 2pm local time underperform their spread by 1.5-2.5 points. Effect compounds when the team is from a different time zone (e.g., West Coast team with 9am body-clock tipoff for a noon ET start). Books underweight circadian disruption in college athletes who lack professional travel infrastructure.

name: ncaab_travel_distance_first_half
thesis: In NCAAB tournament games where one team traveled 1000+ miles more than their opponent to reach the venue, the higher-travel team underperforms their spread in the first half by 1.5-2 points on average. Books set 1H lines as roughly half the full-game spread, but don't account for slow starts from travel fatigue and unfamiliar environments. The edge dissipates by the second half as teams adjust.

name: ncaab_travel_distance_first_half_spread
thesis: Teams traveling 1000+ miles for a road game underperform their first-half spread at a higher rate than their full-game spread, suggesting books underprice the early-game adjustment period for travel fatigue and unfamiliar environments. The effect reverses by halftime as teams settle in, making first-half unders/away underperformance the cleanest signal. Particularly strong for West-to-East travel crossing 2+ time zones.

name: ncaab_travel_distance_totals
thesis: Road teams traveling 1000+ miles for non-conference or tournament games in different time zones show depressed first-half scoring and overall game totals trend Under. College players are more affected by travel than pros due to lack of charter flights, less recovery infrastructure, and academic schedule disruption. Game totals Unders are +EV when the away team has traveled 1000+ miles, especially when crossing 2+ time zones and playing before 2pm local time.
